utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood for the Prosecution, assisted today by our intern, Emma Berry, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my friends from the Prosecution, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and Nicholas Robson, appearing for Rasim Delic, with our legal assistant, Lejla Gluhic, and our intern, Raymond Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I see the witness is in court. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated, sir. Thank you. Mr. Delic [sic] -- I beg your pardon. Mr. Mundis. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell the Court your name, spelling your first and last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: My name is Hamdija Sljuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you could please spell your first and last name for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: H-A-M-D-I-J-A, S-L-J-U-K-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your date of birth, Mr. Sljuka?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of December, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, Mr. Sljuka?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia, and now I declare myself as a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What's your current occupation, Mr. Sljuka?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I am an attorney-at-law, practicing in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions specifically about 1994 and -- between 1994 and 1996. Could you please tell the Court what jobs you held between 1994 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I will try to tell them approximately. Upon an order by the Municipal Staff of Defence of Kakanj, how should I put it, by that order I was appointed deputy commander of security for the Operational Group Bosna with its seat in Zavidovici, in January 1994. I remained at that position until September 1994 or by early October 1994. It was then that the deputy commander for security, Mr. Imamovic, Fadil, was appointed. I was appointed as desk clerk for security with some other three or four desk clerks. At that duty, I remained until the end of September 1995 or towards the end of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Earlier, you said "September/October 1994". Is it now 1995? At line 7, you said: "I remained at that position until September 1994 or by early October 1994." Now, line 11 says until the end of 1995. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the exact date. It was the end of September, early October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... No, I understand. I understand you don't remember the date, but was it 1994 or was it 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of the end of September or early October 1995, I was the desk clerk. My superior, professional superior, was Fadil Imamovic, assistant commander for Security. I remained at that position until the end of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's a big problem here, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I could ask some questions to make this more clear. It might be helpful, considering this is generally non-controversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could lead him through this, it might assist, with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It depends on how your opposite number will respond, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see that across the aisle --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Sljuka, between January 1994 and October 1994, you were assistant commander for Security in OG Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Between October 1994 and September 1995, I think you said the end of September 1995, you were desk clerk in the Security --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: For security, until the end of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And between -- after that, after the end of September 1995, until the 10th of June, 1996, you were assistant commander for Security in the 35th Division; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, to clear up some confusion here that the Judges might have, could you tell us, sir, the difference between the different groups you mentioned, OG Bosna and the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'll be able to be precise in terms of military structure, but OG Bosna was in charge of the units from Kakanj and Zavidovici. When divisions were formed, being larger-scale units -- well, that's it; namely, the Army of BH grew in time and larger units were being formed, divisions and corps. Those were the changes which ensued or, rather, that is what was going on between the beginning and the end of the war in terms of the organisation of the Army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was the 35th Division the successor to OG Bosna?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: One could say so, more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was OG Bosna and the 35th Division -- were they both based in Zavidovici, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, sir, could you tell the Court when OG Bosna became the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: A minute ago, I tried to be cautious with the dates. When the 35th Division was formed, more or less, there were new people appointed, and when I came from Sarajevo on the 30th of September, I came to Zavidovici. An order awaited me there, stating that I was to be security clerk, and Fadil Imamovic was the assistant commander for Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, the 30th of September of which year are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: 1995 -- 1994, sorry. 1994. Given the communication that was in place between Sarajevo and the rest of the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is possible that some of the orders were late, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. You're talking now of 1994. I thought October 1994 to September 1995 you were a desk clerk in the security, you had nothing to do with the 35th Division by that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was all within the Division until September/October 1994. I was with OG Bosna as of September or October 1994. Until demobilisation on the 10th of June, 1996, I was with the 35th Division, and its seat was in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question that you had been asked was: "Are you able to tell us, more or less, when the 35th Division was established?" And then you started telling us about all these positions that you're holding again. Are you able to answer that question, sir, more or less when the 35th Division was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, October 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that helpful, sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In military formation, what corps was OG Bosna in the 35th Division, what corps were they within, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps of the ABiH. Its headquarters were in Buzanica [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you were in the 35th Division, who was the commander of that unit, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Mr. Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could clarify just one thing before we move on, sir. Earlier, you said the headquarters of the 3rd Corps of the ARBiH was in -- and what's written on the screen here is "Busovica." Could you confirm, where was the headquarters of the 3rd Corps, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 3rd Corps was always in Zenica, as of the date of its establishment until it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During the time when you were assistant commander for Security -- I'm sorry. During the time when you were in the 35th Division as a desk clerk, who was your commander, who was your direct superior?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: In terms of command and control, it was Mr. Fadil Hasanagic. In professional terms, it was Mr. Fadil Imamovic for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who was the 3rd Corps commander during this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot be precise. For a while, it was the late General Mehmed Alagic. Later, it was Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more questions about your position as what you've been referring to as a desk clerk. Could you please tell the Court, generally, what were your duties as a desk clerk in the security division, the security department service?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: All tasks that fall within the remit of the Security Service, which existed in all units, starting with brigades, divisions and corps. We received different security-related information, processed it, verified it, and sent it onwards to the superior command, this being the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And in this position, how often would it come to pass that you had to go into the field?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: According to the needs, as was required given the situation that existed within the area of responsibility of my division. If there was any combat, it was possible to have to go to the field more often. "More often" would mean perhaps once every week or on occasion we would even go as seldom as once in two months. Sometimes we had to go once a day. It all depended on the type of problems that had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In compiling the reports that you spoke of, sir, where would you get the information that you would use to write those reports?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Each brigade had its own security organs and its police. The Division had its own security organ and police. All information related to security, the 35th Division security organ received from its own units that were within the 35th Division. The information was put together in a report and forwarded to the 3rd Corps. Information could come from various security organs from the subordinate units or personally gained by the work of us, the desk clerks, gathered in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P02632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit or a document to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That is -- well, it's a document to be tendered. It's a "P" number, Your Honour. It has not yet been tendered, so it is P02632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court generally, is this the sort of report or of a type or sort of report that you would produce in the department, that is, the Security Service of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: This is not a report. This is an official note. Could I please be shown the second page? There should be a signature there. This is an official note drafted by the desk clerk Fikret Skejic. It contains the information he gained in the field, and it was forwarded to the 3rd Corps. In addition to such official notes, we also sent out daily reports to the Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what position did Fikret Skejic hold in relation to your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I see here the 18th of September, 1995, he held the same position as I did, desk clerk, and in addition to him being there, there were other three desk clerks, Mehinagic Ferid of Maglaj, and Husnija Marusic of Zavidovici, and Husein Mujkic, aka Mujkara, of Zavidovici. There was also an assistant commander for Security, Fadil Imamovic; the technical assistant or secretary to Fadil, I cannot recall her last name; and the IT person who worked on the reports. I think his name was Fuad Terzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could this exhibit please be admitted into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you please explain to the Court what was the duty of the Military Security Service in relation to POW that had been captured?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Any combat order contained -- or rather every combat order contained a chapter that had to do with security. As regards the Division, we had orders in place on the treatment of POWs. Each unit that captured an enemy soldier were supposed to have him delivered to the 35th Division police, and then that person was supposed to be escorted to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was the relation between the 35th Division police and the Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: What do you mean, "relation"? The police were controlled professionally by the Military Security Service. All instruction, in terms of professional work, was given by the Military Security Service, in terms of orders, directives, professionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, sir. I'm going to ask you some questions now about some units that were in the AOR of the 35th Division. Did you come to learn anything about the El Mujahid Detachment during your time as a security officer, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I can't be precise in terms of dates, of course, but as for the El Mujahid Detachment, I cannot tell you exactly as of what date it was within the area of responsibility of the 35th Division out of all the units that were there. I think it was from the end of 1994 until the end of the war or, rather -- how should I put it? Until the truce was signed or, rather, the Dayton Accords, all units from within the Army of B and H were linked in terms of security and concerning the area that I worked on. All of the units were included in the chain except for the El Mujahid unit. That unit had no security organ of its own with which the Security Service of the 35th Division --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: But first I want to show you a document that might help clarify things about dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could Exhibit -- I'm sorry, could document P01863 please be shown to the witness. Can you see this document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what does this document tell you about the movement of the El Mujahid Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: This document describes the relation within the -- between the Corps and the OG North. I can only comment in terms of what I can conclude from this document that I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll ask you specifically about the line: "Established line of defence and the unit detachment, El Mujahedin, according to the decision of the unit commander, move it to another region." Can you tell me, sir, before the El Mujahid Detachment was in the AOR of OG Bosna, in what area of responsibility was it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know of the El Mujahid Detachment while it was within the area of responsibility of OG Bosna or the 35th Division. I don't know whether that unit was anywhere. I don't know that. I know that they came from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The date of this document, sir, if the English could be scrolled up a bit, I believe it's 6 November 1994. Does this correspond with what you remember about when the El Mujahid Detachment moved into the area of responsibility of OG Bosna?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No. Of OG Bosna, it could only have been arrived then. As far as I can remember, they came into the area of responsibility of OG Bosna towards the end of 1994. It is possibly related to that, but I don't know. I apologise. As of January 1994, I was with OG Bosna, and at that time there was no El Mujahid Detachment. They may have come towards the end of 1994. As to where they were before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor has not established a sufficient base or has not established a link between the witness and the document. Another thing, the document is not known to the witness. This is apparent. And facts within the document are not known to the witness, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, that's a pretty high standard, Your Honour, considering -- and inconsistent, I think, with the standards that we've been used to in this court. The witness did indicate that this does appear to be a document from the ABiH, and he did indicate that the information within it appears to be consistent with what he recalls, generally speaking, about the movement of troops at the time. I believe that the Prosecution has established sufficient grounds for this to be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's easy for anybody to say this document comes from the ABiH, because one looks at the document and can read that. We've been asking that there must be a link between the witness and the document. The witness also doesn't know anything about the facts written in the document. I think you've got to establish a link, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, perhaps it would be most expedient to have this marked for identification. Another witness later might be able to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll do that. May the document be marked for identification and be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 624.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told the Court that you believe -- you've told the Court that you believe the El Mujahid Detachment came into the area of responsibility of OG Bosna late 1994, early 1995. Can you tell the Court, how often did you have contact with anybody in the El Mujahid Detachment during your time after 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. First of all, the basis should be established, and it must be determined whether the witness had any contact before he's asked how frequently he had contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you have contact, sir, with any members of the El Mujahid Detachment in your capacity as a member of the Security Service?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: A minute ago, I tried to explain this. With regards to security matters and affairs, I had no contacts with the El Mujahedin Detachment, because Security Service members are appointed and vetted, that they are professional people with integrity, honest people, it couldn't be known who is who and who does what in that detachment because they did not have any military hierarchy. So I could not receive any information about security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Hello, sir. Mr. Witness, can you look at me? Hello, sir. The question simply is: "Did you have any contact with the El Mujahedin Detachment?" And I think you can answer that confidently with either "yes" or "no." Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment named Aiman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you please tell the Court a little bit about Mr. Aiman? For instance, what language did he speak?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: What I learned about him was as follows: He lived before the war in the area of the former Yugoslavia, that he had studied medicine in Rijeka, that he was married to a woman from the area of the former Yugoslavia and that he was fluent in Bosniak. I did have some contacts with him, mainly whenever the El Mujahid Detachment was passing from Zenica to Zavidovici and from Zavidovici to Zenica. After the Dayton Accords there were check-points at the entrance to Zepce which was controlled by the HVO, and at the exit of Zepce there was a joint check-point of HVO and the Army of BiH. All units had to announce their passage through the HVO-held territory, which means that each passage of the El Mujahedin Detachment or members thereof had to be announced to Security Service by Aiman, and then the Security Service would announce this to the Zepce security officer so that they could pass through that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a follow-on question to that, sir. At page 15, line 15, you said: "This was after the Dayton Accords." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No, the Washington Accords between the Army of BiH and the HVO, the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When was the Washington Agreement -- when did it come into force, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: In February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall, generally speaking, when was the first time you had contact with Mr. Aiman?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely over the phone when this was, but also I personally met him. He would drop by the Security Service maybe to make arrangements for tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. He would stop and talk to the police officer within security. Somebody would -- from our Security Service would speak to him. Sometimes it was me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I would like to ask the witness the following: When you would meet Mr. Aiman, what function would he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which function he exercised, but he spoke Bosniak and he, as I stated previously, he spoke to Security Service because the Security Service was in charge of announcements being sent to the HVO security officer in Zepce so that their passage can be arranged. As far as his function was concerned, I don't know which it was. That detachment had no military hierarchy, they had no insignia. I don't really know which post he occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You described -- well, first of all, let me ask you, sir, you said you don't remember exactly when you had your first contact with Mr. Aiman. If I could maybe help to clarify that a bit. Did you have any contact with him in 1994?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Contacts could have been by phone or on the premises of my Security Service, where it was located. In 1995, I personally met him once when I attended a meeting at the Corps. I was driving back, stopped in a cafe to have a coffee, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I appreciate the comprehensiveness of your answer, but my question is a more simple one. Did you ever have contact with him in 1994?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot claim. I may have -- in person, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I mean any contact over the phone or in person.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Over the phone, yes, concerning the passage of the -- that detachment, as I have explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you explained there were these check-points in Zepce, that it had to be cleared ahead of time before troops could go through that check-point. Was this the same procedure that was followed when other ARBiH units had to pass through that check-point?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The delineation line between the HVO, Zepce, and the Army of BiH, looking from the direction of Zenica and from Zepce towards Zavidovici, there were two check-points. If you're going from Zenica, the entry check-point, the exit check-point, on the one there were BiH Army soldiers manning it, at the other HVO soldiers. That arrangement applied to all Army of BiH units, including the El Mujahedin Detachment. Everything had to be pre-announced. If I may add something. Since members of the El Mujahedin Detachment did not speak our language, a very strict time slot had to be arranged so there would be no problems or no conflict erupting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You spoke earlier of contacts with Mr. Aiman on the telephone and also in person. Could you tell the Court generally, how often would you have contact with him, either on the phone or in person?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot state precisely how frequently, but each passage of theirs had to be cleared in advance. There were five or six of us in the service. Sometimes I would take the call, somebody else would on other occasions, maybe once or twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Other than to arrange passage through the check-point at Zepce, did you ever have any other contact with Mr. Aiman?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I remember one occasion when we talked about the problems that we had detected among the El Mujahedin Detachment members. In Zavidovici, we had a rule prohibiting soldiers to carry rifles, and the police of the 35th Division carried out such controls, but the El Mujahedin Detachment members disregarded this order and they moved around, disregarding the curfew as well. Once, I spoke to Aiman about that, and I received his assurances that they will cease with such practice, that they would be sanctioned, but I could not tell him who the perpetrators were, since they did not come from our part of the country and they were very difficult to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a follow-on question to something you said earlier. At page 18, line 12, you indicated, sir, that: "Sometimes I would take the call, somebody else on other occasions, maybe once or twice a month." I just want to ask, sir, what time period are you speaking about when there would be contact with him, that is, Mr. Aiman, once or twice a month?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period and exclusively about the period while the El Mujahedin Detachment was in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now, sir, some questions about the Military Security Service and its role in handling POW. You explained a little bit about that earlier. I'm going to ask you some questions specific to specific incidents now. Do you recall, sir, how many times, during the time that you were in the 35th Division or OG Bosna, did the Military Security Service deal with POW, that is, process captured POW?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Of the Security Service of the Operational Group and the 35th Division did not have the task to process war crimes. Security Service had a task of safely and securely transferring POWs to the 3rd Corps, where experts or professionals would establish and document whether somebody had committed war crimes or not. Our Security Service had no hand in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did the Military Security Service safely and securely transfer POW during the time when you were with the 35th Division, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I personally took part in -- on two occasions. In the first case, we had two members of the Army of Republika Srpska, and on the other occasion, three captured members of the Army of the Republika Srpska. I cannot recall whether any other clerks or my commander worked on such cases. I personally had occasion to talk maybe for an hour or two with a professional JNA lieutenant originating from Bosanska Krupa, then another --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but it might be easier if we could go through this step by step. Now, you said there were two occasions. Can you say generally, sir, on the first occasion, what month and year was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: In 1995, both cases, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And the first occasion, do you recall what month?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, those two POWs may have been captured in June or July 1995, before the Vozuca pocket, and the other three were captured during the Vozuca operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, sir, when was the Vozuca operation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember after so much time that has elapsed, maybe October or November. I'm not sure. Maybe September and October, maybe the 10th or the 11th month of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you were saying, at page 20, line 6, you personally had occasion to talk for an hour or two with a professional JNA lieutenant originating from Bosanska Krupa. Was this one of the POW you dealt with in July or was it one of them that you dealt with in September?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That was the group captured at Vozuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was this the only POW that you were aware of who was captured or who was rumoured to have been captured in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I did not hear the witness say that prisoners of war from September 1995 were discussed, so this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood. Can you also explain the use of the word "rumour"? I'm not quite sure I understand why that crept in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. As to the objection, I don't understand exactly the basis for the objection. The witness did say that this professional JNA lieutenant that he spoke of was captured in September, in relation to the Vozuca operation. I don't know how it can be more plain than that. And as for the question of "rumoured", I can ask him a more specific question along those lines, Your Honour, to make that more plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the witness say this lieutenant was captured in September during the Vozuca operation or did he just say "during the Vozuca operation," and therefore you inferred that it must be September because that was the time of the Vozuca?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he did say it was during the Vozuca operation, and he did say, as far as he remembered, that it was September or October, maybe the 10th or 11th month of 1995. I'm quoting now from page 20, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have seen that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I have not understood you correctly, so I would like to clarify this point. I understood that he was talking about two prisoners. The first time he was dealing with POW, this was either in June or July -- July, rather. And from what I understood, that particular prisoner was a prisoner who was one of the first two prisoners he saw on the first time. I would like you to clarify this for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell the Court, as to the prisoner you spoke of in July, was that the first time you had come into contact with POW during your time in the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Her Honour Lattanzi said and repeated what the witness had said, that he spoke to this witness in June or July, and now that June or July has become "July" in the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat the question. The POW that you came in contact with in June or July 1995, was that the first time you had come into contact with POW during your time in the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I personally for the first time worked with prisoners of war then. It was maybe in July. I cannot be precise, but it was before the Vozuca. We received, from one of the brigades, two prisoners of war. The police of the 35th Division transferred those two prisoners of war to Zavidovici, and this was my first contact. This was my first personal case of prisoners of war. The second contact occurred after the Vozuca operation. I cannot specify the date, but I am sure because I drank coffee with those people at the office, we watched television, and we discussed matters from the day he came to the Bosnian territory after -- he explained to me that after the Croatian war he was transferred to Titograd and then he was given an order that all people originated from Bosnia should go fight in Bosnia. I spoke to those people. They spent the night, because it was quite late, and for at least one and a half hours I smoked and had coffee with those people in my office or, rather, in the premises of the police of the 35th Division. We discussed matters. They would ask what is going to happen to them. I explained to them that they are going to be exchanged. That officer asked me whether it would be possible for him not to be exchanged. I explained to him that he could remain in the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of them was a lawyer, a secretary of a court --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. We do have limited time, and I want to ask more questions about some other incidents, though I do appreciate your answer. Now, other than this person you're speaking of, did you ever come to hear that any other POW had been captured during the Vozuca operation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot be certain and claim so, but there must have been, because more people were exchanged than the number of people that I saw personally. And after the Dayton Accords, all sides had to release detainees or prisoners of war from the military detention centres. The number of people exchanged was higher than the number that I just stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever have any specific information that other units might be holding POW?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: In my statement to the investigators, I said that in accordance with some rumours or stories, the El Mujahedin Detachment held a number of captured members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Do you recall, sir, where this information came from?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was; it was a state of war. Maybe I heard it in the town of Zavidovici or maybe I heard it from soldiers. What had to be done was to verify the veracity of such rumours. As far as I could remember, in order to verify such unsubstantiated information, I was tasked with going to the El Mujahedin Detachment to see for myself. I cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you. You said you cannot recall the date. Can you tell us was it after or before the Vozuca operation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: How do I explain this? I am quite uncertain as to whether it was before or after. From this position here, I cannot tell you whether it was before or after the Vozuca operation. It could have been before, it could well have been after. I cannot say anything for certain. I probably drafted the report on that. Should you find such a document, perhaps that would jog my memory a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, it's your testimony that you don't remember whether it was before or after the Vozuca operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty whether it was before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you had given a statement to an investigator; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you remember when that statement was given?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: On the 5th of July, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was your memory of these events fresher in 2005 than they are today, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: It's about that date, that time, I couldn't remember the other two POWs. It was only yesterday that I recalled that. Of course, I allow for the possibility that it was before as well as after, but I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Would it refresh your recollection, sir, to be able to take a look at the statement that you gave to the investigators earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let us clarify something. Did the witness provide the statement in 2005 or is it the statement that we have, since we only have one statement with a different date than the one mentioned by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and thank you, Defence, for bringing that up. It is dated 2006. The statement I have is dated 2006, 7 July 2006. The witness told me yesterday he believes that that was taken in 2005. Near his signature it says "7/7/2006". This is something that we can perhaps clear up with the witness, but in any event we are speaking of the only statement that I'm aware of that he gave to the OTP, and that is the statement dated July 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, clear this by talking to the witness rather than testifying, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Sljuka, there is some confusion about when you gave this statement. Can you tell, was it in 2005 or was it in 2006?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I think I gave the only statement, and this is the statement mentioned by the Prosecutor, but however I think the date is wrong. As far as I recall, I gave the statement in July 2005, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you gave the statement, did you sign the pages, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, was it a written statement, sir, that you gave in July 2005, before we talk about signing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in English, and it was read back in Bosnian. I signed it. I believe that it was in 2005, when I opened my office. I think it was in 2005. And then I observed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's stay one point at a time. My question was: Was it a written statement or was it oral? You said it was written. My next question to you: Did you sign that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, and this is the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. You have answered me. Once you said, "Yes," you've answered. When you're saying this is the statement, which statement are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it was in July 2005 or July 2006, I don't know, but it is the same statement. I gave that statement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, thank you very much. If you were shown a copy of a statement, would you recognise it? I'm not quite sure, Madam Vidovic, based on your objection, whether you object to him being shown a statement, a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We do not dispute that. We merely wanted to see whether the witness gave just one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Let's put it on the e-court so that everybody knows what we're talking about, e-court or ELMO, whatever it is. Sir, can you recognise that handwritten -- wait a minute, let's look at the handwritten part first. Can you recognise that? What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my signature and the date of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the date there, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 7th of the 7th, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we turn all the pages for the witness, let him see just that handwritten part, sir? Turn over the pages. I thought we were going to turn over the pages there on the ELMO. You see the signatures there? Next page. Just check them all and see whether they are all your -- yes, carry on. Okay, I guess that's enough. Can you then look at the first page. The first page, the heading at the top of the page. You do read English, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then there's no point in you looking at that document. You may carry on, then. I don't have a B/C/S copy of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So just for the record, sir, is this the statement you provided to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it must be, and it was me who was wrong about 2005. This must be the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, would it help to refresh your recollection if you were able to see this statement you provided in 2006, as to the date when you visited the camp? And if I could draw your attention particularly, sir, to paragraph number 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, the document just given to the witness, is that the English statement or is it the B/C/S statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I apologise for not clarifying that, Your Honour. Yes, that is the translation of this English statement into a language that the witness understands, that is, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read paragraph 51, sir? Does that refresh your recollection about when you might have visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The document put before me contains certain information about the El Mujahid Detachment. When I gave this statement, I referred to some other things. Perhaps this was the reason why I mentioned it in the statement. I don't know whether I referred to any other particular document, or the one mentioned here, or whether I referred to any other information that was in circulation about the El Mujahid Detachment when. When I visited them, I don't know if it was September. I said here it was 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just look at paragraph 48 of your statement, sir. I think that's a better paragraph to look at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you stand by that statement that you have made on paragraph 48 today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned on several occasions here that it was in September. I am not certain now whether it was in September, indeed, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, listen to my question. My question is: Do you stand by the statement you've made in paragraph 48 as you sit there now? Does that reflect your recollection of the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not certain whether what I stated was at that time or at some other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you went to the camp -- well, first of all, let me back up. I just want to make clear you were tasked with going to the barracks of the El Mujahid Detachment. Was that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who told you to go there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I truly fail to understand this line of questioning. First one needs to establish what the facts were pertaining to different things and whether he did, indeed, receive a task. This is a most leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I think that comes from the statement of the witness himself at paragraph 48, and the question was: "When you went to the camp -- well, first of all, let me back up. I just want to make clear. You were tasked with going to the barracks of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Was that your testimony, sir?" I think by "testimony," really it should be, "Was that your statement?" So it comes from the statement, and then the question followed, "Who tasked you?" Are you going to stand up?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I insist on my objection. First, it has to be established whether he received the task by someone, because that's not what the witness said. He did not clearly state that he stood by the statement exactly. First we need to establish what had happened, why he went there, who said what. Otherwise, we fail to understand the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't understood you well. I understood that the only uncertainty he had was with regard to the date, if it was in September 1995 or another date. Can you confirm this? Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So has the objection been ruled on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I see the time is 10.20. This would be an appropriate time, in the course of the examination, to take the break, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So be it. We'll come back at quarter to 11:00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move on to a different topic now. To confirm, you became assistant commander for Security for the 35th Division at the end of September 1995? Was that what you said in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And that's the position you held until you were demobilised, until 10 June 1996, just to confirm that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court briefly, what is the role of the Military Security Service in investigating crimes?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The Security Service is a body that deals with security issues within the given unit. There was a criminal investigation department within the military police, with qualified people, investigators, and people who would, after having assembled statements and information, would draft criminal reports and forward them to the military prosecutor's office. Their domain covered only military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As assistant commander for Security, what knowledge did you have of what reports were being sent to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: In principle, I offered professional help to the criminal investigations department of the military police. It had to do with crimes committed by military personnel on duty. It had to do with property crime, deserting, murder and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Let me ask my question in a different way. Were you aware, sir, of any reports going to the military prosecutor about specific crimes like, for instance, murder or property crime?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I don't know during which period it was exactly, but it was me who was drafting criminal reports. I drafted about a dozen, and they were later processed by the military court. Sentences were handed down up to five or seven years' imprisonment. Just to add, since the military court and the military prosecutor's office had many cases on their hands because of the war, some crimes were processed more -- faster and some were received as criminal reports. What ensued was a general amnesty for certain types of crimes where people were not prosecuted, and those that had their trials initiated were acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You said at page 32, line 21, you don't know which period it was exactly, "but it was me who was drafting the criminal reports," and I'll ask that now. What period was it exactly where you were drafting criminal reports, when you drafted about a dozen criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: It was before I came to the 35th Division, when I was assistant commander for legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I'm speaking specifically now about when you were assistant commander for Security in the 35th Division, sir. What was your knowledge of the criminal reports that were going to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: If the police dealt with such cases, I don't know what the outcome of the proceedings was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, sir, I'm asking specifically about the reports. What was your knowledge of the reports that were going to the military prosecutor, that is, from the people in the Military Security Service beneath you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: On each criminal report submitted by the criminal investigations department, the Security Service would be informed as to the name of the person and the crimes allegedly committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you speak of each criminal report submitted, can you tell us, what general category of crimes were these?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: It was the crime of illegally selling weapons, deserting a unit, theft, property crime, and similar offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you ever know of criminal reports submitted by investigators to the prosecutor for the crime of murder?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I know of one murder in Zavidovici. It was processed by the 328th Mountain Brigade. There was a murder in which one soldier of the brigade was killed by another soldier of the same brigade. Proceedings were initiated against that person at the military court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, when you say, at page 34, lines 7 to 8: "It was a murder in which one soldier of the brigade was killed by another soldier of the same brigade," can you clarify for us, sir, which brigade are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the witness said the 328th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear of any criminal reports being filed for any crimes committed in the Mujahedin camp that you alluded to earlier that you had visited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. This question implies that certain crimes took place, and that is not what the witness ever mentioned. The question implies certain crimes having been committed which deserved a criminal report to be filed. The witness did not mention that by a single word, and there is no basis for such a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood, I think the formulation of your question suggests that crimes were committed in the El Mujahedin Detachment, and you haven't established that through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware, sir, of crimes that were committed, if any, in the Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Personally, I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So as the organ in charge of criminal reports and referring them to the military prosecutor, were you aware of any crimes that had been committed in the Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I will correct myself to a certain degree. I don't know whether any crimes occurred within the El Mujahedin Detachment. However, I do know that when one POW was being transferred, and he was a member of the VRS, as he was handed over to a unit of the 35th Division, and that was the police, several members of the El Mujahid Detachment kidnapped that soldier, and a report was drafted. That took place in September 1995. The Military Security Service filed a report with the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where did this event take place, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That POW, in September, was being transferred from one of the units, I believe from the 328th Mountain Brigade, to the Military Police of the 35th Division. When he was being handed over at the gate of the 35th Division's barracks' perimeter, several members of the El Mujahid Detachment kidnapped that man and drove away with him in their vehicle. This was the information given to me by the military police, and the Security Service informed the 3rd Corps about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where was the 35th Division barracks?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The command of the 35th Division was at the post office building in Zavidovici. This incident took place at the military police barracks, which was quartered in the former kindergarten in Zavidovici. So the Command of the 35th Division was on the right-hand side of the Bosna River and the military police was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether anybody was ever charged in connection with this kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I don't know what ensued. The report was drafted. As for any measures being taken, I am not familiar with those. I don't know what happened subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You say a report was drafted. Was that a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No, it was informing the 3rd Corps. I cannot submit reports against unidentified people. We have to know exactly what their name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Finally, sir, during your time in the 35th Division, were you aware of any member of the Mujahedin Detachment being charged with any crime committed anywhere within your AOR?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot be precise in terms of date. I know that a member of the El Mujahid Detachment was brought before the court when they attacked an official. They attacked a colonel, I believe, of the Nordic or the Polish Brigade. It was in Zenica. And they were also charged with theft and robbery in Zenica. However, I cannot recall at what time that was. It was outside the Division, and I am not certain whether it was still during the war or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you say "the Nordic or Polish Brigade," what general organisation are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: When they were passing through, I don't know, it was SFOR at the time or something else, but when they went on the road, by certain El Mujahid Detachment members in Bukva, the incident followed. A colonel was attacked and proceedings were instituted, and I believe those people were sentenced by the Zenica Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So can we take from your answer, sir, this is the only incident that you can recall in which a member of the El Mujahid Detachment was charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: As I said, there were instances in Zenica, but I'm not sure whether this was during the war period or post-war period. I cannot be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is Zenica within the area of responsibility of the 35th Division or was it during the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Well, the 3rd Corps was headquartered at Zenica, and that is the superior command of the 35th Division. The seat of the 3rd Corps was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, before you conclude, since the witness's statement has not been entered into evidence, I would like you to follow up on the question that you put, yourself, to the witness about the visit to the El Mujahid camp. You asked him about it, and he did say that he was tasked with going to the El Mujahid camp, but we never heard if he actually went and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could have just one moment to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your indulgence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sljuka, we talked before about you were ordered to go to the El Mujahid camp. Can you tell the Chamber, please, did you go to the camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And perhaps it might be helpful if you could tell the Court generally where this camp is located.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The El Mujahedin camp was located somewhere mid-distance between Zavidovici and Kamenica, some ten kilometres from Zavidovici up the Gostovic River towards Kamenica. It was located in the Gostovic River valley at a plateau. There were several abandoned homes of Serbs who had left. Those houses were destroyed. There was a number of tents erected there, used by the El Mujahedin Detachment. It was their military camp or their barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what happened when you got to the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Pursuant to the command of either the 35th Division commander, Mr. Fadil Hasanagic, or the assistant commander for Security, Mr. Fadil Imamovic - this means I don't really remember who gave me this order - I went to the El Mujahedin camp, and in my conversation with members of that detachment, I was to ascertain whether they had any captured members of the VRS. Upon arriving there that day, I went to the gates, accompanied by a driver and two military policemen with the insignia of captain first class. We stopped our vehicle before the gate. This is the tarmacked road between Zavidovici and Kamenica. On the right-hand side, level with the road, was a gate. There was a bar. And two El Mujahedin Detachment members stood by that ramp. When the vehicle stopped, I made a couple of steps towards them. Two military policemen exited the vehicle and stood by the vehicle. I tried to establish some contact, but they did not speak Bosnian. I mentioned Aiman, and I tried to find somebody who spoke Bosnian. I was told that he wasn't there. One of those persons went to a tent, and another person, who spoke Bosnian, came to me. Therefore, I established contact with that person. I told them about my intentions, the intentions of my superior command, what I was requested to do and what we need to ascertain. I asked them -- I asked -- rather, I told them that we had information that that detachment held a certain number of prisoners of war. I explained to them how prisoners of war should be treated, where they should be held, and that they should not be held by units. I explained to them that there was a pending exchange, where the 7th Corps was planning an exchange with a unit of the Serbian Army, that the Bosnian Army had no prisoners of war, and that the VRS held civilians, so if there were any prisoners of war, this matter should have been sorted out as soon as possible. That person went back to a tent, summoned by somebody else, so that person was absent for a couple of minutes and then came back, and what he provided to me were assurances that they had no prisoners of war, that had they some prisoners of war, they would have handed them over. What I could see with my own eyes on that plateau, I could see all the tents, and I saw 10 to 12 members of the El Mujahedin apart from those on the gate. Some people were fetching water. Some people were washing themselves. And from what I saw, I could not determine whether or not they had any captured POWs. I told them that we had information that there was a captured woman, and I explained to that person, my interlocutor, that the conditions had to be so and so, given that the prisoner of war was a woman and they had a duty of care and they should stick by such rules, but that person told me that there were no prisoners of war, that the camp contained only El Mujahedin Detachment members. And upon hearing that, I returned back to Zavidovici and reported back to the instance that issued the order. I must have drafted a report to the 3rd Corps Military Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you tell the Chamber, please, did you ever go into the camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No. I was in front of the gate, from which point I could see the whole area that they used, all their tents and all the facilities that they used, but I did not enter the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: From your vantage point, the gate, could you see into all the tents and into all the building?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: There were no buildings there. There were destroyed houses and barns without roofs, of inhabitants of Serb ethnicity who had left for Vozuca. I saw two tents which were open, and that person I spoke to when he went back to that tent, there were sleeping bags lined up there, but I could not see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: These two tents you speak of, were these the only two tents in the camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: There were four or five, but those two tents which were closest to the gate were the only open ones, and they were empty. As far as I could see, there were no persons in there. There was some other tents -- how can I explain? The perimeter was 100, 200 square metres, and the tents were located on that plateau. There was no proper gate. There were two poles with a bar placed across those two poles, serving as the gate, and this is the place where the vehicles entered and left the camp, and of course they walked in and out of the camp through that gate. And that gate was level with the road between Zavidovici and Kamenica, and the gate was located some five metres away from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: On page 39, at line -- beginning at line 18, you said that when you got to the gate, you told them "we had information that the detachment held a certain number of prisoners of war." Did you ask at that time or at any time to go into the camp? And just for your clarification, sir, I'm speaking of the transcript. I'm not speaking of your statement. I see you're looking at your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Perhaps if that could be removed from in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I first came to the gate and when my vehicle stopped, that is, those two persons manning the gate, let's call them "sentries" or "security," they had their rifles hanging from their right shoulders. When the vehicle stopped, one of them approached the vehicle with the rifle slung across the shoulder, and the other person pointed the rifle at the vehicle that we were in. When I explained I wanted to speak to the man in charge to discuss matters, I was told to wait. One of the sentries went to the camp to look for somebody speaking Bosnian, and he entered several tents. He came back with somebody who could not speak Bosnian fluently but with whom I could communicate, and it is that person that I spoke to at the gate. I did not insist on entering the camp because I was told that I should wait and that somebody would be coming to the gate. And as my conversation with that person progressed, I received information and I did not enter the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After you returned to the headquarters in Zavidovici, as you testified earlier, did you do anything else to try and follow up the information that there were POW in this camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I could not find out, on the basis of rumours and after my visit to the camp. I personally did not learn or could determine that they had any prisoners of war from the point of my visit afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You testified earlier about contacts that you'd had with a particular member of the El Mujahid Detachment, Mr. Aiman. Did you at any time ask Mr. Aiman about this rumour that there had been POW in the El Mujahid camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I discussed with him this issue. I can't remember whether I discussed this matter with him. I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, the Prosecution has nothing further at this time, unless Your Honour has specific questions. Thank you, then. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sljuka. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. I'm going to question you on behalf of the Defence of General Rasim Delic. And since we speak the same language, please, after each of my questions, you pause a while for the interpreters to have the time to interpret my question and then your answer. The nature of cross-examination is such that most of my questions can be answered with a "yes" or "no," so please, whenever possible, do so. You told us that you provided a statement to the investigators of this Court on the 7th of July, 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I must comment on this. It must have been a mistake. I provided one statement, maybe erroneously wrote "2006". I still believe it was 2005, but this is the statement. I gave no other statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However things may be, you gave that statement and this is what you recall?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, in that statement, described -- and I invoke paragraph 10 of your statement. You referred to the very difficult situation in the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you worked in in 1994-1995, including Zavidovici and the wider area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a couple of questions specifically concerning that situation. In that area, before military activities of Vozuca and Ozren in 1995, is it correct, is it not, that Zavidovici, before the July and September operations in 1995, were in a very difficult position?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were encircled by Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those Serb forces daily shelled the area of Zavidovici and other Muslim villages surrounding the town from the area of Vozuca and Ozren?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: And Blizna, which was the closest to Zavidovici, and they held -- they could see Zavidovici as they could see the palm of their hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The area of Tuzla was shelled from these areas as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those shellings had horrendous consequences; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to see D582. This is a video. The interpreters have a transcript of that video, so the interpreters will be able to read the transcript. It is video 10.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Oh, what have they done? An expletive. "In the late afternoon today, we once again visited the clinical centre in Tuzla, there, the battle for the lives of the seriously wounded citizens of Tuzla continues. The Cantonal Minister of Health, Dr. Kasim Muminhodzic, gave us the latest information concerning the state of the patients accommodated at this clinical centre. Let us say right now that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French booth just told us that they did not receive the transcript or the French translation, so I would maybe expect them to interpret directly from what they hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Oh, what they have done. "In the late afternoon we revisited the Clinical Centre in Tuzla, where the battle for the lives of the seriously wounded citizens of Tuzla continues. From the Cantonal Minister of Health, Dr. Kasim Muminhodzic, we received the latest information concerning the state of the patients accommodated at this clinical centre. "Let us say right away that the number of killed is 66, while the list of those who were seriously or lightly wounded last night has gotten longer; namely, 176 citizens were wounded. Dr. Muminhodzic told the journalists that in the course of last night, a total of 241 persons were received and accommodated in the Clinical Centre as well as in other health institutions in this town. The fact that 66 of those were killed clearly shows the dreadful proportion of the Chetnik crime against the youth of Tuzla. "Otherwise, while fighting to save the most seriously wounded, there has been an intensive effort since last night to identify the young men and women from Tuzla who were killed. Thanks to the immense efforts of the medical teams and the help of the families of those killed, 63 persons have been identified so far, while the identification of the three remaining citizens of Tuzla continues. During the day in Tuzla were organised a number of extraordinary ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljuka, you knew of this incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This happened on the 25th of May, 1995, on the occasion of the prom night of high school students in Tuzla. I was in Zavidovici when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was not an isolated incident; such shellings from Ozren were an everyday occurrence in the area of Zavidovici and the wider area which included Tuzla. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Sljuka, my question concerning this incident is as follows: Many incidents such as this, with very grave consequences, did take place. Did you ever hear that this incident was prosecuted, that somebody was held to account for this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: As far as I know, families of the victims still insist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I rise to my feet to object to the form of the question. It doesn't really seem like a question at all, in fact. At 46.23: "Many incidents such as this with very grave consequences did take place." That sounds more like a statement than a question to me, Your Honour, and I would object on those grounds; that is, specifically, the legal grounds are: No foundation and relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, this is a cross-examination. My suggestion to my witness is that many such incidents did take place which had not been prosecuted. As for relevance, it is twofold. In this case, I am trying to prove that my client issued a legitimate order or, rather, he approved a legitimate military action, through his directive, which concerned the Vozuca pocket. That's one matter. The other matter is the question that I'm coming to, and that refers to the capacities and capabilities of military security to investigate such incidents as this one which occurred in the same area, at the same time, with horrendous consequences, and which they did not investigate. And this is the relevance of my question. May I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
