utterances.text: No, don't. Just let me comment. First of all, Madam Vidovic is cross-examining, and she's obliged to put her case to the witness and get the witness to comment. I don't think there is anything wrong in her saying that there were many such incidents. Madam Vidovic, your client is not charged with approving a military action in the Vozuca pocket, so when you say that: "As for relevance, it is twofold. In this case, I'm trying to prove that my client issued a legitimate order or, rather, he approved a legitimate military action through his directive which concerned the Vozuca pocket," he's not charged with that, ma'am. So I allow the question, but if the purpose is to show that the approval by your client was legitimate, then that's irrelevant because he's not facing that charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I still have another issue I'd like to discuss. During the examination-in-chief, incidents in which the soldiers from the ABiH would have been involved and investigations -- and criminal investigations were conducted into these incidents, this was mentioned. But in this particular case, the incident was caused by the enemy, so I would like to understand how there can be a connection between this question and the questions put by the Prosecutor during its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, this is a part of the Defence thesis, and it is not directly linked to the questions posed by the Prosecutor. It is our case here that I have the right to develop further during my cross-examination. Second of all, there may have been a slight error in interpretation. Therefore, I'll try to answer Judge Moloto's question again. As regards what I said, that the Vozuca operation was a part of the directive issued by my client, well, what I'm trying to establish with this witness is this: Whether the military security services of the area, including his own, had the ability and means at their disposal to investigate such incidents, including the incidents from the indictment and including the incidents such as this one, with horrendous consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Madam, with what is raised by Judge Lattanzi, which is that this witness cannot tell us about the capabilities to investigate crimes on the part of the VRS army. He didn't work for the VRS army. I thought this clip is talking about atrocities committed by Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are correct, but as you will see, as will be confirmed by the Prosecutor, according to the rules, the Bosnian Army security services were duty-bound to investigate such incidents and they had to establish who the victims were, disregarding the fact that this incident or this crime was committed by the opposing party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They may have been obliged, in terms of the rules, to investigate, but in terms of this case, was it their responsibility to investigate those cases and punish them, punish the perpetrators? That may be a reason, in terms of their rules, for purposes of keeping statistics of their casualties, but is it relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, they were duty-bound, and I don't mean the witness specifically, but the security organs were duty-bound to submit criminal reports for each and every crime. Why is it of relevance for this case? I'm trying to prove that even as grave incidents as this one, which happened in the same area and at the same time, was not investigated, no report was submitted, since they had no means and ability to investigate it and to establish the facts. And I will try to clarify that with the witness by putting one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I still have an issue with this. I know full well that as far as credibility of the witness is concerned, you are putting all the questions you would like to put and can put in any manner you wish to put, because you would like to test the witness's credibility. But as far as substance is concerned, you should nonetheless establish a connection with the examination-in-chief, and I don't see this connection. When you put this question, you are talking about investigations into actions caused by the enemy, so to my mind this question cannot be admitted. This is my own personal view.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Your opposite number is on his feet, unfortunately. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I think another thing that is worth pointing out here, Your Honour, is that we have heard testimony about the area of responsibility in this case of the 3rd Corps and in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. This does not fall into the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, which makes this line of questioning all the more irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Madam Vidovic, you may respond, including to that last point.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first and foremost, I'll respond to the latest portion. This shell was fired from Ozren --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you are testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was relevant, since it concerns the same area and the same period of time. It displays -- it illustrates the facts which I'm trying to test here that had to do with the indictment. These facts pertain to the events within the framework of the indictment. Another thing concerning cross-examination: It is my deep belief that Defence is allowed to pose questions in addition to the questions pertaining to the witness's credibility, to put questions which are in favour of the thesis of the Defence, as Defence sees them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I've heard your argument. I'm going to allow your questions only because you say you want to establish the existence or lack of capabilities within the 35th Division to investigate these problems. That is the only basis, really, that the question can be allowed. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was about to put that question when I was interrupted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw the footage and you said that no one was prosecuted, although the victims' families demanded that. My next question is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That becomes a problematic question. Is it for the 35th Division of the BiH Army to prosecute criminals within the VRS, unless they've caught them as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is precisely what I'm trying to clear up. I will ask certain questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you're talking about prosecuting these people from the VRS who committed these crimes. I thought I'd said to you your question becomes relevant to the extent that you want to establish that the 35th Division didn't have the capability to investigate these problems because, in terms of the rules, they would have to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is true, is it not, that security organs, including the security organs of the 35th Division, were duty-bound to gather information on a crime committed within the AOR, be it that it was committed by a member of the Army of B and H or a member of the VRS, so that they would be able to submit a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My next question, thus, is the following: Many incidents with horrific consequences were never investigated because the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the 35th Division, had no means to undertake appropriate investigations; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: You are. May I comment? We had no technical means needed to carry out an on-site investigation and to document things. We had people who were there but were not professionally trained, so if one looks at their professional expertise, some of them were carpenters, locksmiths, people working in the field of economy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get to that later, Witness. Your Honours, before that, could we please assign an exhibit number to this footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to this being admitted into evidence, again on grounds of relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe the footage is very relevant to the thesis of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have a problem with this, and in light of what's been said, namely, that this came under the responsibility of the 2nd Corps and not of the 3rd Corps, but beyond that I also wanted to acknowledge that the witness this morning did mention investigations that did take place. Therefore, I still have a problem understanding the line of questions put by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The clip is -- sorry, the objection is overruled. The clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 625.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will go back to your field of work. Before the war, as far as I could see from the background information on you in the statement given to the prosecutors, to the investigators, you stated that you were a judge at the Court of Associated Labour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also worked as an assistant commander of the Territorial Defence Staff for Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, for legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then as of 1993 onwards, you worked as a desk officer for security?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to put the following to you: You are an experienced lawyer. However, you will agree that you had no military knowledge before working at the positions you held within the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had no knowledge or experience from within the competence of security organs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I encountered that for the first time when I was assigned to those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your associates from the security organ of the 35th Division, as you began describing, had no knowledge or experience concerning security issues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We see -- we saw the document drafted by Skejic, Fikret. What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: He was a locksmith. He worked at the metal factory in Krivaja. He was a qualified locksmith.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Husein Mujkic's profession? He also worked with you, as you said.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: He worked on prefabricated houses. He was a carpenter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Ferid -- I cannot recall his last name. What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Ferid Mehinagic. Before the war, he was in the Natron company in Maglaj. He was a qualified locksmith.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was Husein Marusic's profession?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Marusic, Husnija.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: He was a clerk for economic affairs. He would draft a report sent to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single member of your Security Service section had specific training such as it existed in Serbia, in Pancevo, before the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct, they had none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff and the corps organised various training sessions for those people, but you will agree, I hope, it was insufficient to compensate for the lack of knowledge they did not gain through education or previous experience.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct. Those were one- or two-day sessions, and not everyone attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the situation demanded that such people be placed at those positions, since you had no other personnel?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The services of the military security functioned according to the principle of subordination?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Battalions had a person tasked with military security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then brigades had desk officers for security or assistant commander for Security, depending on the type of brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All brigades within the AOR of the 35th Division had their own security organ, with the assistant commander of the brigade for security, during 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The security section of the 35th Division was supposed to receive reports from security officers of the brigades on all important events from within the AOR of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Summaries were made, in terms of information, and sent onwards to the corps or, rather, to their security section?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Simultaneously, the division commander would be informed on important events pertaining to his work?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to put some questions to you concerning the duties of subordinate commands and their security organs and their remit and competence, given the fact that you were also asked about that by the Prosecutor concerning the submission of criminal reports. I wanted to ask you this: You will agree that the obligation to report, which we discussed a minute ago, was supposed to follow the line of subordination? It was not the only obligation of the subordinate command, specifically of a battalion or brigade, when it comes to events from within the area of activity of the brigade; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You'll agree with me, won't you, that security organs of battalions or brigades, if they were to receive information about an event which would fall within their remit, they would be duty-bound to be concerned with that event and investigate it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, they would have to take concrete steps in terms of investigating such events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is not incumbent upon them just to report on events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Working on security matters, it is known to you that there was a rule -- rules of service for security services within the armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Security Service had certain competences from the area of counter-intelligence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This included detection, surveilling, documenting, and preventing activities of intelligence services, particularly military intelligence services, against the armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, this also included the creating of the pre-conditions for as complete documented as possible when it comes to war crimes and other criminal offences in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Military Security Service also performed some functions pertaining to staff security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within this competence, a military security service would assess the security situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, and would inform the commander of irregularities detected.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, on the basis of conclusions from security assessments, Military Security service, apart from informing the commander, service [indiscernible], had to take measures falling within its remit?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which included giving proposals to superior officers of appropriate measures that the superior officer should take in the system of control and command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, Military Security service had jurisdiction concerning military police affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that this included professional direction and guidance of authorised personnel within the military police in pre-criminal investigation proceedings?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we show Exhibit 585 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before it appears on the screen, Witness, let me ask you: You must have seen this document. This is the rules of service adopted by the Presidency on the 11th of September, 1992. You told us that you knew these rules, and at this point I would like you to take a look at page 13 of the B/C/S version, which is at page 9 in the English version. Please take a look at paragraph 40 and 41. But for the record, let me just say I'm not sure whether it can be seen in the English version -- can we scroll down, please? Witness, do you agree that this chapter is entitled "Military Security Service in Criminal Proceedings"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at the provisions of paragraphs 40 and 41. You can read them to yourself. And in the English version, paragraph 40 continues on the next page. And let me ask you - and I presume that you've read paragraphs 40 and 41: Do you agree that these provisions of the rules of operations of the Military Security Service, namely, paragraphs 40 and 41, have the effect of Military Security Service of brigade command and their superior Military Security officers propose criminal reports to the Military Prosecution Service if there are grounds to suspect that a criminal offence, falling within the jurisdiction of military courts, had been committed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So they must take steps to apprehend the perpetrator and to secure evidence and other information that may be used for a successful prosecution or for a successful conduct of criminal proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will continue dealing with these rules of service, but I believe that the time is right for taking a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we discussed the competences of military security organs at brigades and lower levels; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that if a military security organ of a brigade were to come upon information of a criminal offence falling within the jurisdiction of a military court, it is incumbent on that organ to obtain information on that event and to refer those to the competent military prosecutor; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They would be failing in their duty if they simply wrote a report to the superior command; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is incumbent upon such an organ to secure the evidence of criminal offences and the basic information available to them because they are the closest to the event, in terms of area and time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They are closest to the perpetrator of the criminal offence in question; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were it otherwise, that information would be going to the superior command and then to another superior command, and this would be a waste of time in order to secure evidence, et cetera, and information; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put this document away, Your Honours, because this has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I'll just mention the military prosecutors. Working at Military Security, you must know that during 1992, a decree having an effect of a law was passed on District Military Courts and District Military Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to see Exhibit 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm discussing the decree law on District Military Courts. You know that the Presidency adopted such a decree in the Presidency of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Republic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we take a look at page 4 of the B/C/S version, but let's first have the witness see the date of this decree, when it was adopted. And the page in the English version is 11.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: The 13th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, is it necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the 13th of August, 1992? I don't think there was a question that sought that answer. Oh, the date of the decree. Okay, sorry. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. May page 2 of the Bosnian version be shown to the witness, page 2 in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at Chapter 3, "Jurisdiction of District Military Courts."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Bosnian version enlarged a bit, this relevant portion, Articles 6 and 7, please. And the English version, could it be scrolled down so that we see both articles? Well, yes, Article 6 is on this page and Article 7 on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at Article 6 and, after that, Article 7. Read those to yourself, and then I'll ask you some questions. In connection with this, I would like to ask you this: You will agree, won't you, that military courts, during the period of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had jurisdiction to try criminal offences perpetrated by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct, and this is how they proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They also held jurisdiction to try civilians if they committed criminal offences against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its property; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now please take a look at page 3 of the decree in Bosnian, and that would be page 7 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Can we enlarge this text?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we enlarge Article 25 under "Special Provisions." It is towards the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see, Witness, the special provisions on criminal proceedings before district military courts? Please read this article. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we scroll up to the next page, the next column. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this provision lists the competences and the tasks and powers stipulated by the Law on Criminal Procedure, and under item 3 it says that those of the organs of the Interior will be carried out by authorised officials of the security organs of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and military police organs within their prescribed jurisdiction. Witness, in other words, when a criminal offence falling within the jurisdiction of military courts is perpetrated, then the organs of the Interior that would otherwise be in charge if these concerned civilians, that security organs take over jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, together with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the military police organ within their prescribed jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this means that they collect evidence, which means organs of military security, and submit and file criminal reports; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By the same token, they are obliged to file a criminal report to the district military prosecutor; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, can we put this document away, please. It's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you will agree with me, won't you, that the pre-war penal code, the Penal Code of the SFRJ, has been taken over by the Republic through a decree before the war, and you're a legal professional, you know about these things?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes. That, and other laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can we have the witness take a look at Exhibit number 3. That's the Penal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Can the witness be shown the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is the law that the Bosnia and Herzegovina republic took over as the Penal Code of the Republic at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, for the jurisdiction of criminal offences which were tried at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Well, what we're interested are criminal offences that were regulated by the Penal Code of the SFRJ. Can we take a look at page 87 in the Bosnian version and 93 in the English version, please. In the Bosnian version, 87.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in the Bosnian version, please. The English version is okay. Can we have the next page in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see that this chapter is entitled "Criminal Offences against the Armed Forces of the SFRY," but this was amended to read: "against the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to see this page, but first we have to state this: Do you agree that Article 201 regulates failure or refusal to carry out an order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then refusal to accept or use arms, that's the next article, and especially the following Article 203, which regulates the matter of insubordination. Well, let's take a look at page 104 in the Bosnian version and 109 in the English version. So 104 in the Bosnian version. Page 104, the first article on the page. Let's have the title. Witness, can you see?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: "Failure to report".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that would be the following page in the English version. That's 109 in the English version, page 109.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this is "Failure of Duty to Inform Military Organs". So you saw the criminal offences listed in this law, and you would agree that the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which was then taken over by Bosnia-Herzegovina, envisages a range of criminal offences which protect the principles of line of command and control and command in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this document into evidence? Oh, I apologise. It has already been admitted, it has an exhibit number. It can be put away, unless the Bench have any questions concerning it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only thing is, ma'am, that I would like to understand is: The document, in English that I see on the screen, is titled "Failure to Carry Out Duties During Mobilisation." You referred to Failure of Duty to Inform Military Organs," and I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe you can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now I can see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please put this document away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document may be put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Within the area of responsibility of the 35th Division, its brigades had military platoons, did they not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 35th Division also had a platoon of military police of their own?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No, a company.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, a military police company. How many military policemen does it mean within the Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Around 100 policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct in thinking that in Zavidovici, there was a military police battalion as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I cannot be precise, but we always refer to them as the company of the military police of the 35th Division, and the battalion of the military police was with the 3rd Corps. This company was probably part of that battalion, but, in military terms, I cannot be any more precise. However, the company was larger in terms of numbers than the platoons in battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion of the military police, for which you said was within the 3rd Corps, were they quartered in Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Occasionally, there was contact and information was exchanged, in professional terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the military police, it is true, is it not, that the use of the military police could be ordered by the unit commander within which that military police unit was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, I'm also correct in saying that the use of the military police could also be suggested by the military security organ?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The competent military security organ?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now a few questions regarding the functioning of the military security in the 35th Division. It is true, is it not, that the orders which had to do with combat activities always contained a chapter pertaining to security situation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, inter alia, orders defined the tasks of the military security?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: An order for combat activity included instructions on how to treat POWs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The treatment of POWs in accordance with the relevant Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Such orders also regulated the accommodation of such POWs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, Your Honours, I would like to show D154 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: D584 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, it is a General Staff document dated the 35th [as interpreted] of August, 1995. Among others, sent to corps commands and military security sections. It is titled "Instruction --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter said "dated the 35th of August." I haven't experienced that date before. I see it's called the 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now? It is possible that you have never seen this document, but I wanted to ask you something about certain facts mentioned in this document. Could we scroll down so as to be able to see the whole item 1 which has to do with the processing of POWs. Please have a look. Do you agree that by virtue of this document and its item 1, it is described how captured enemy soldiers should be treated so as to keep that in accordance with the application of rules of International Law of War which had been sent previously as part of an order of the General Staff concerning any -- concerning the application of the International Laws of War?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also agree that this came via the Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document by the General Staff -- I apologise. Witness, we have to slow down. Do you agree that item 2 of this document of the General Staff states -- or rather regulates the work of military security when researching and documenting war crimes and the crime of genocide?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By the same token, what is mentioned is the obligation to put into practice the order of the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have a look at the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can see the top of the page. What is mentioned here is that the Staff needs to implement the orders of the 17th of July and of the 7th of April which were sent downwards by the Security Administration of the General Staff. Do you agree that the subordinate units received this instruction by the Security Administration concerning the treatment of POWs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: They must have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know who Jusuf Jasarevic is?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: He was the chief of the Security Administration within the General Staff of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could we assign an exhibit number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 626.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Exhibit -- no, actually, it is D585 -- to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the document. It is a regular combat report by the 3rd Corps and the 3rd Sabotage Detachment. Today you mentioned certain POWs that you met. I believe it was in September. Please have a look at the first paragraph so as to be able to establish whether you actually were referring to these POWs. There is a mention here of two officers, a captain and a lieutenant. That is what reminded me of your previous answer. Is it possible that these were the two POWs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Most likely. There was a lieutenant, there was a captain, and there was a second lieutenant and a reserve officer in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Sead Rekic signed this. Can we scroll down in order to be able to see the signature. In English, it is page 2. We cannot see the signature quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, Your Honours, we can give a Bosnian copy for your perusal. Perhaps on that copy we can see the signature better. Here, it was cut in half when copying the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it says "Dekic," I believe. Yes, perhaps you can see it clearly on our copy. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, and thinking about it, most likely it was Sead Rekic's unit that transferred those people to the 35th and Division military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, let us go back to chapter 1. In this document, it states that -- that is, paragraph 1 --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence, read it to yourself. In the English, it is the first chapter, Your Honours. You can see there that it states that: "During the day, the reconnaissance group which was based near Ljajevac --" Well, I can't read very well since I have given my copy to the witness. However, it is stated here that the POWs were treated in accordance with the corps commander's instruction, and two officers are mentioned. It is mentioned here that, according to the document, four Chetniks were taken prisoner, two of which were officers, a captain and a lieutenant, and that they were treated in accordance with the corps commander's order concerning prisoners.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I'm certain that I was talking about those mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that this document shows, does it not, that units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina reported on the treatment of POWs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whether they were treated correctly or incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they were duty-bound to report on that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we assign an exhibit number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have but a few questions left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When giving your statement to the investigators, in paragraph 39 of your statement of the 7th of July, 2006, you describe the treatment of POWs as follows: "Specifically, if I would refer information that a POW was taken by any unit, and if I would hear that the regular procedure was not followed, I wrote up information about it also saying that I would continue with further action about that. When I say that, I mean that I would check whether it was true or whether somebody was just boasting with such information." I quoted your statement to the investigators of the OTP, and I wanted to ask you this: Have I understood well that if there was information on irregular treatment of POWs, you would report on that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would be duty-bound to do so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, first check information, establish what the case was, and then report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given that there were irregularities, you were also duty-bound to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, procedure as prescribed. If the information were true, if it was proven to be true, then further measures would be undertaken which fell under the competence of the security military -- military security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those further measures would mean conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed another thing. You said that first you would try to establish whether someone was merely boasting concerning that information on POWs. That is why I would like to ask you the following: It is correct, is it not, that subordinate units occasionally sent information on far greater numbers of captured soldiers or killed soldiers on the enemy side, which did not correspond to the reality of the situation, trying to boast or, rather, give a wrong picture of their successes in combat?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes. There were reports from subordinate units which were unreal, unrealistic. Subsequent checks would confirm that this did not correspond to the situation on the ground. It was during the war, and then certain units would try and boast by stating that they had liberated a certain portion of the territory, whereas it wasn't true. That is what I had in mind, and that is what I tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to clarify something for the record. It is page 75, line 17 and 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you this. I asked you about exaggerating the number of people taken prisoner and those killed. I asked you whether they were trying to inflate their successes, and I apologise, this is line 12 to 14, page 75. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: It happened, did it not, that subordinate units would inflate the number of enemy soldiers killed and taken prisoner so as to inflate their success during the combat activities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like you to see another document, Exhibit 480.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, this is a report of the 328th Mountain Brigade that was shown to you by the Prosecutor, while you were providing your statement to the investigators. That document is dated the 13th of September, 1995. This is a regular daily combat report. Please take a look at the addressee of this report. It will be KM or the command post of the 35th Division of land forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness the second page of this document, and the following page or the last page, which bears the signature. That would be page 5 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you is as follows: You may remember that you made comment on something which the Prosecutor showed you today, that you said that after seeing this document, you went to the El Mujahedin Detachment's camp. What I'd like to ask you in connection with this document is as follows, please: Did you receive, down the line of command through security organs, any information about the prisoners of war being kept at El Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that I did not receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So through the line of subordination from the military security of brigades to the military security organs of the Division, that you did not reach such document or information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour, as a follow-up to the last question asked by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, you said you can say with certainty that you did not receive information down the line of command through security organs of any information about prisoners of war being kept in the El Mujahedin camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: In connection with this document, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What information did you have when you were ordered to go to the El Mujahedin camp in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. My cross-examination in connection with this document was limited to the line of communication through the military organs from subordinated to superior organs. What Mr. Wood is doing is that he is reopening his examination-in-chief on the information that he received prior to going to the camp, so this falls outside the boundaries of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I think the record will be deeply confusing if this question isn't clarified, Your Honour. I don't think this goes beyond the scope of the cross-examination, and I'm in no way trying to reopen my direct examination. I think that this is just something that is confusing and that needs to be clarified. The testimony is that the witness went to the camp. He must have had some information. I just seek to find out what that was, for the clarity of the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want to find out whether that came through the lines of communication or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, then, the question will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, the question asked before was what information you had when you went to the camp. Perhaps it might be helpful also, considering this, to explain where you got this information from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's different from what I asked you. If you were going to follow up what I asked you, you would then ask the witness where he got the information from that tasked him to go to Gostovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, Mr. Sljuka, I'll repeat the Judge's question. Where did you get the information from that tasked you to go to Gostovici?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I stated clearly that there were unverified rumours, so what must -- what had to be determined is whether they were true or not, and this is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must interrupt you, sir. You were not tasked by a rumour. Some official tasked you to go to Gostovici. Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, either the commander or assistant commander for Security. So division commander or assistant division commander for Security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is your answer, Mr. Wood. You may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing further, Your Honours. I just wanted to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us, during the examination-in-chief, I believe, that there was an amnesty as regards criminal offences that may have been committed by armies -- soldiers of the ABiH Army. My question runs as follows: The amnesty related also to war crimes, did it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No. It was a law on amnesty for specific criminal offences, criminal offences against prisoners of war, genocide, and criminal -- war crimes, rape. This was not encompassed by the amnesty, or criminal offences punishable by 20 years in prison and more. Some criminal offences were exempted from amnesty. Amnesty specified criminal offences which it applied to, but war crimes were not part of the amnesty. The law on amnesty did not encompass those criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One other small question. You told us about your visit to the Mujahedin camp when you stopped at the front gate. What I wanted to know is: Had you wanted to go inside, would you have been able to? Would you have had the authority necessary to entitle you to walk inside?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: When the vehicle stopped at the gate, let's call it a gate, although I described what it was, I emerged from the vehicle with two military policemen. The driver remained in the vehicle. And we were met by two sentries at the gate. When I explained that I was looking for the person in charge, they told me, "Wait until the person in charge arrived." That conversation took place at the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that I had understood, but I was wondering: Had you wanted to go inside to check and to see whether the prisoners were there, maybe they weren't, would you have been entitled to go inside?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I was told to stay put there, and I remained there. I was not allowed to go inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Witness, please do answer the question. Listen to the question and answer the question that is put to you, please. You're not asked what you did. You're asked what authority you had.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: To go to the El Mujahedin Detachment. I went there, and I was clearly said, "Stay here, wait at the gate," and I waited for somebody to talk to. That interlocutor conducted the conversation with me at the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you decided to believe what you had been told; you decided to react like that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Otherwise, because the other side dictated the terms under which and where we would be having the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you did not have the authority to dictate your terms, did you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, both parties have, during their examination-in-chief and cross-examination respectively, referred to the statement offered by the witness on 7th July 2006, and I was just wondering if I could invite the parties to elicit information on one of the pieces of information which are included in the witness's testimony. And I was specifically thinking of the information contained in paragraph 40 of the witness's statement, in which Mr. Sljuka states that apparently the El Mujahid Detachment was not in the chain of command of the ABiH on the same terms, at least, as other ABiH units. I would like to invite the parties to find out from the witness what he means by this part of his statement, because I think this would be crucial to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I can also put the questions directly myself, if you prefer to do so. Very well, both parties seem to be in agreement with this. Mr. Sljuka, can I ask the Registrar to pull up the witness's statement of 7 July 2006, if that is possible, so we can show the -- is that not available in the e-court system? I understand that the statement is not included in the e-court system. Then could I ask that a B/C/S copy be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a copy here. I can hand it to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Sljuka, I kindly ask you to go to paragraph 40 of your statement. Have you read it, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I wish to know what you mean when you say that only those ABiH units who were strictly in the chain of command of the ABiH are the units that you have referred to, and then you continue to say that exceptions to this is the El Mujahedin Detachment: "I had no information on their activities." Can you tell us what you meant by this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: My statement refers to the line of command of security organs from the lowest level of units to the highest level of units. I explained that each battalion had a security organ, brigades had security organs, and a division had a security organ. The exception to this was the El Mujahedin Detachment, which -- with which we never had established contacts with respect to the security organs, that we could verify information with and from, and this is the only unit that we had no such security organ in, and this is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Nevertheless, you say that, in the line just above this, that you only were referring to ABiH units who were strictly in the chain of command of the ABiH. This seems to suggest somehow that you did not consider the El Mujahid Detachment as being within the chain of command of the ABiH. My question to you, sir, in respect of this statement of yours: What were you told by your superiors, if anything, about the position of the El Mujahid Detachment in the chain of command of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I don't know precisely what kind of contacts the Command had with them with regard to a line of command and command and control. What I'm referring to here is from the -- in the light of security organ functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, let me put my question more directly to you. Did you consider the El Mujahid Detachment to be an ordinary part of the ABiH, on the same footing as other units within the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I know the detachment was there, which means it was an autonomous detachment, in my knowledge. I know that they did not fit in the control-and-command line as other units of the ABiH. Those who commanded units know more about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you discuss with any of your superiors your lack of means to communicate with the El Mujahid Detachment about security issues, and which instructions were you given to this -- in this matter?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Well, everybody in the Security Service knew about that. First of all, first you have to appoint a security organ, and the 35th Division security organ must know the identity of that person so that they can contact that person, because apart from regular combat reports, we had security reports up and down the line. So if you do not have a person appointed to be your contact, a person to receive confidential information, then you have nobody to communicate with within that unit, either orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that, but I guess it would be natural to try and seek some information from the El Mujahid Detachment on security issues, so if you did not receive any written regular security reports from them, which you say you did not, then one would have sought to elicit this information from your contacts with Mr. Aiman, perhaps. So my question is: Did you seek information which would otherwise have been included in the security reports, from Mr. Aiman?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: What we wrote down about that unit is what we learned from our own organs. They had no insignia. They were not regular -- like regular soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whenever we sought something from them, then they would respond, "Oh, yes, of course, you will receive that," but there would be nothing following and you had no means to determine whether some things or matters were resolved or not. And all information that we learned about them were included in our information going to the 3rd Corps. Well, you could not stop and ask an ID of a person who did not have regular military documents, so if an MP were to stop somebody to determine whether a person is on a sick leave or is deserting or is on his rest-and-recreation time, this was possible with those -- with regular soldiers, but this could not be done with the El Mujahedin Detachment members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Apparently not. But your answer seems to suggest that you did, in fact, include some information relating to security matters about the EMD in your report to the Division Command. What was this information; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Well, I can remember the disregard for the curfew, then carrying rifles, or incidents concerning people sunbathing and bathing in the river during summer, or incidents concerning the socialising of men and women at the same place. There were such incidents. I can't remember, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any action was ever taken as a result of your reports about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I remember that there were cases where El Mujahedin Detachment representatives would promise to 35th Division representatives that there would be no further cases of irregularities, so the 3rd Corps' reaction was that these matters had to be resolved, and I know of such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is crucial evidence. Are you saying that the 3rd Corps did exercise its authority to raise these security matters with the EMD and that the EMD -- sorry, the El Mujahid Detachment did, in fact, respond to these calls from the 3rd Corps; is that a correct understanding of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: I don't know how you understood it, but we would include information about irregularities permitted by El Mujahedin Detachment members in our report, and we would try to resolve problematic situations together with the 3rd Corps people dealing with security issues or morale issues of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, I had meant to ask you questions about this further, so I am going to ask you those questions. Sorry that we have to go through the same territory once again, but I have slightly different concerns. My first concern, sir, is: Based on this sentence at paragraph 40 that: "When I say units, I exclusively refer to only those ABiH units who are strictly in the chain of command of the ABiH," and then you carry on to say: "An exception to that is the El Mujahedin Detachment," my question to you is: Why do you then include information about the El Mujahedin Detachment in your reports to the 3rd Corps if, according to you, the El Mujahedin Detachment was not strictly in the chain of command of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Because they were located in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. But then why then do you say: "They would not report to us and I never did nor tried nor could establish contact with them"? They are in your area of responsibility. If everything that is in your area of responsibility is your responsibility, then you must try to make contact with them, shouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: When I mentioned the security organ a while ago, such organs communicated and coordinate with each other. I never received any information from my superior command that that particular unit had any security organ, and it was never requested that any information be passed on to that unit. That's why I said I had no communication whatsoever with the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Then you were tasked to go to Gostovici, and you have told us your experiences when you got there. Did you give a report to your security organ or to your superiors on your visit to Gostovici?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it oral or in writing?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Orally, I was to inform promptly the person who had issued me with that task. I must have submitted a written report as well. Somebody from the Security -- to someone from the security Services of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the substance of your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: That on orders, whether it was from the commander or the assistant commander for Security, I visited the El Mujahedin Detachment, trying to establish whether the unit has a certain number of captured enemy soldiers on the premises. In contact with an unidentified person who speaks Bosnian, I learned this and that. I describe it, I mentioned the answers I received, and I must have mentioned in the report what had happened. More or less, it amounts to what I told you. You would find the same thing in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you have your own independent impression of whether or not there may have been prisoners of war in that camp?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: As I said, I tried to survey the camp as far as I could see, trying to make any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We haven't got much time. Did you have your own independent impressions, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: It was not my impression that at that moment they had any captured people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, just before we get off, I'm sorry, I'm not able to say what the exhibit number is, but I just want to -- if we could show the witness the order subordinating the El Mujahedin Detachment to the ABiH, please. It's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That could perhaps be Exhibit 396, Your Honour. If we could have a look at that, that might be what you have in mind, Your Honour. Or perhaps if that's not it, Exhibit 431, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just see the order part of it, please. This is a resubordination order. I want an order that -- anyway, this is an order, anyway. Sir, I would like you to look at just paragraph 1 of that order and then look at the signature of the -- the signatory to the order. Before we go to the signatory, I would like to see the date of this document. 2nd June 1995. Can we see the signatory, please. Okay. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You realise -- would you still stand by the statement you're making, that this El Mujahedin Detachment was an exception to the other units that were subordinated -- that were in the line of command of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA SLJUKA
utterances.text: This document came from the 3rd Corps commander, Mr. Mahmuljin. It is a combat document, such as the ones I did not encounter at the time. Independently of that, it is still my opinion that irrespective of any orders, one couldn't do anything with that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is a resubordination order. I actually wanted the order that established them and subordinated them to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. We will look for that order, Your Honour. And for the record, just so it's plain, the order that he was looking at just then was Exhibit 396; is that correct, Mr. Registrar? I see that that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anyway, we've gone beyond our time. I'm afraid you'll have to come back tomorrow. Tomorrow, the hearing is going to be in Courtroom III, not this courtroom, and it's going to be at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Okay, sir? So make sure that you come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom III. Court adjourned.
